claims.text: A two-phase coexistence molecular-dynamics approach is an efficient alternative to full ab initio free-energy thermodynamic integration for computing melting properties of refractory materials.
The initial material is a crystalline refractory alloy below its melting point.
The method uses a simulation cell containing coexisting solid and liquid phases.
Molecular dynamics is performed with an interatomic potential calibrated to DFT data.
The coexistence simulation should be conducted near the expected melting temperature and at nominal pressure.
The simulation cell must be large enough to sustain a stable solid-liquid interface.
The solid-liquid interface mediates phase equilibrium.
The solid-liquid interface allows energy and volume changes associated with melting to be determined.
When solid and liquid phases coexist, the system naturally converges to the melting temperature.
The interfacial energy balance provides the latent heat of fusion.
The entropy of fusion can be obtained from the latent heat at the melting temperature.
The difference in volume between the solid and liquid phases gives the volume change at melting.
The method yields melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, and volume change at melting.
The predicted melting properties will agree acceptably with results from ab initio free-energy integration.
The coexistence approach has significantly lower computational cost than ab initio free-energy integration.
The method's accuracy depends on the quality of the interatomic potential.
The method's accuracy is affected by finite system-size effects.
Extreme conditions or subtle phase behavior may be represented less precisely than by full DFT-based integration.
The two-phase coexistence approach is widely used and less expensive than full ab initio methods.
Its results can vary by several percent relative to full ab initio methods depending on simulation parameters and potential quality.
